summary: Lists security threats related to IPv6 multihoming. Multihoming may create opportunities to redirect packets to unintended addresses. The document looks at threats common to all solutions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Having two doors makes a house easier to enter, and also gives a sneaky person more places to try. This memo lists risks that come with connecting through multiple roads.

subtitle: Security risks when sites connect to the Internet through multiple paths

tldr.problem: IPv6 multihoming allows a site to connect through multiple Internet paths, but this creates new opportunities for attackers to redirect traffic to unintended destinations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs threats that apply to all multihoming solutions: redirection attacks that send packets to an attacker, black-hole attacks that drop traffic, third-party denial-of-service, and privacy risks. It frames the problem as proving ownership of network identifiers when locations can change.
tldr.outcome: By understanding these generic threats, designers of specific multihoming solutions can ensure their protocols defend against them, avoiding a patchwork of vulnerable deployments.

facts.label: Application security classes
facts.value: 5 identified classes with different threat profiles

facts.label: Main threat categories
facts.value: Redirection, black holes, DoS amplification, address spoofing

today: RFC 4218 remains an informational reference for IPv6 multihoming protocol designers. It has not been obsoleted and continues to be used to ensure new proposals address known security threats.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4218 examines security threats that arise when a site (or host) connects to the Internet through multiple different paths simultaneously or switches between them dynamically. The goal of such multihoming is to improve reliability and performance without requiring the site to get multiple globally routed IP address blocks, which would make the routing system larger and more complex.

The central security concern is redirection attacks: the ability for an attacker to cause packets meant for the site to be sent somewhere else instead. Redirection can lead to confidentiality loss (eavesdropping), integrity damage (modifying the data), or denial of service (dropping the traffic). The RFC examines threats that exist in all multihoming solutions, not specific proposals, to provide guidance for protocol designers.
sections.plainLanguage: When a site uses multiple connections to the Internet, an attacker might trick packets into going to the wrong place. This memo lists all the ways that could happen.

sections.title: Today's Assumptions and Attacks
sections.content:
The RFC reviews existing attack vectors in today's Internet, which multihoming solutions must not make worse. Applications today rely on DNS to look up addresses, routing to deliver packets, and in some cases, cryptographic security (IPsec, TLS) to bind to a specific peer. Attackers can already manipulate DNS and routing to redirect traffic, but cryptographic defenses prevent them from impersonating the legitimate endpoint.

The RFC identifies five classes of application security configurations, from public content servers (caring mainly about integrity and availability) to systems using strong cryptographic identity binding. Each class faces different threats when multihoming is added. Additionally, the RFC distinguishes between on-path attackers (who can see and inject packets on the route) and off-path attackers (who can only send forged packets). The analysis assumes on-path attackers have full packet-manipulation ability, though monitoring vs. blocking capabilities may differ in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: Today, bad guys can already try to trick you with fake DNS or broken routes. But if you use passwords or encryption, they still cannot pretend to be your bank. The question is: does multihoming make new tricks possible?

sections.title: New Attacks from Multihoming
sections.content:
The RFC catalogs several new threats enabled by multihoming. Redirection attacks cause packets to flow through an attacker; an attacker might learn secrets by sniffing, or modify data in transit. Time-shifting attacks involve using old, replayed messages to trick a host into changing addresses. Black-hole attacks redirect packets to a place where they vanish, denying service to the legitimate recipient. Third-party denial-of-service attacks make a multihoming solution help the attacker amplify attacks against unrelated victims.

Accepting packets from unknown locators is another threat: if a multihoming solution is too permissive, it may receive traffic from addresses it did not expect, causing confusion about which peer is communicating. Privacy concerns also arise when multiple address changes over time leak information about a user's location or movement patterns. The RFC emphasizes that defense must bind communication to a permanent identifier, not just the current network address.
sections.plainLanguage: The new tricks include: sending your packets through an attacker, making your packets disappear, helping an attacker hurt someone else, and leaking where you are moving.

sections.title: Identity and Authorization
sections.content:
The core defense is to ensure that only the legitimate owner of a network identifier can change which addresses are associated with it. The RFC describes this in two complementary ways: the site must authenticate itself and prove it is authorized to control a particular identifier, or it must prove ownership of the identifier and thus be allowed to control its locators.

Applications and transport protocols must bind their security decisions to the identifier, not the current address. If a host can change addresses but application-level security binds to the old address, an attacker can hijack the connection. This means multihoming solutions must work with, not against, existing security mechanisms like IPsec and TLS, ensuring they remain bound to the right peer even when network paths change.
sections.plainLanguage: The fix is to make sure that before someone can change where your mail goes, they prove they own your mailbox. And your mail should care about your mailbox, not the current mailman.

sections.title: Scope and Incomplete Threat Analysis
sections.content:
The RFC explicitly notes it is incomplete: it does not analyze any single proposed solution in detail, and it does not cover multicast QoS, connectionless protocols, or specific threats to the identifier-to-locator binding mechanism itself. Any actual multihoming proposal must do its own detailed threat analysis in these areas.

The document assumes that at some point, key parts of the Internet (DNS, routing, security protocols) will have some level of security in place, and a multihoming solution should not become the weakest link. It also assumes that application protocols either do not care about the identity of the peer, or they have strong cryptographic security. Intermediate cases where an application uses weak host-based authentication need special attention.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo does not give a full answer; each new multihoming proposal needs to check all these threats carefully and explain how it defends against them.
